theme: Jacob to Egypt; Israel settled in Goshen
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 46:1-47:31. Jacob and the whole family, seventy people, make the long journey down to Egypt. They are settled in Goshen. Jacob meets Pharaoh. The years pass, and Jacob prepares for his death.
settingTheScene: The famine continues. Jacob, now an old man, packs up the entire family and heads to Egypt. On the way, God appears to him at Beersheba and confirms the move: “Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation.” Joseph rides out to meet his father after twenty-two years. The family is settled in the region of Goshen, the best of the land. Jacob is presented to Pharaoh. The years pass. Jacob, near death, makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan, not Egypt.
observation: Jacob stops to offer sacrifices at Beersheba. He is honoring the place where his father Isaac had also encountered God.
God speaks to Jacob in night visions, calling him “Jacob, Jacob”, affectionate repetition.
Verse 46:3: “Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation.” This fulfills Genesis 15:13.
The list of seventy persons (46:8-27) is the foundation of Israel. Seventy is a number of completeness.
Joseph rides up in his chariot to meet Jacob. They weep together. Twenty-two years of separation.
Jacob is presented to Pharaoh. He blesses Pharaoh, the lesser blessing the greater? Or the patriarch blessing the king?
Jacob’s life, “few and evil have been the days of the years of my life”, is candidly described as hard.
The famine grows severe. The Egyptians sell their flocks, then their land, then themselves to Pharaoh in exchange for food.
Israel settles in Goshen, prospers, and multiplies (verse 47:27).
Jacob, near death, makes Joseph swear with the same oath Abraham used, to bury him in the cave of Machpelah.
interpretation:
These two chapters cover the final settling of the patriarchal family in Egypt. The descent into Egypt that began with Joseph as a slave now welcomes the whole family as honored guests. The four-hundred-year sojourning that God predicted to Abram in Genesis 15:13 has officially begun.

Notice the careful way the move is framed. Jacob does not just rush off to Egypt. He stops at Beersheba, the place his father Isaac worshiped, and offers sacrifices. He pauses to seek God’s blessing on the journey. And God meets him. In a night vision, God speaks: “I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation. I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again.” This is one of the most important promises in the patriarchal narratives. God is going down to Egypt with them. The God of Canaan is not bound to Canaan. He travels with his people. And he commits to bring them back. The descent is real, but it is not abandonment.

The list of the seventy who came to Egypt is the foundation of Israel. The biblical writers will refer to this number repeatedly. Seventy elders will accompany Moses to Sinai. Seventy disciples will be sent out by Jesus. The number marks the people of God, small, complete, gathered.

The reunion between Joseph and Jacob is brief but powerful. “Joseph presented himself to him and fell on his neck and wept on his neck a good while. Israel said to Joseph, “Now let me die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive.”” Twenty-two years of grief and waiting end in a single embrace.

Jacob is presented to Pharaoh. The exchange is striking. Jacob “blesses Pharaoh” both at the beginning and end of the encounter. Hebrews 7:7 says, “It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.” The aged patriarch blessing the king of Egypt is a quiet but powerful statement of who really represents the God of heaven. Jacob’s life is described candidly: “Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers.” Jacob has not had an easy life. He acknowledges it. But he stands before Pharaoh as a man of God.

The famine policy section (47:13-26) is one that bothers many modern readers. Joseph collects all the money from Egypt, then all the livestock, then all the land, in exchange for food. By the end, the Egyptians have sold themselves into Pharaoh’s service. Joseph is implementing what is essentially a transition from a free society to a centralized monarchy. The text describes this without moral comment. The full implications will become visible only later, when a new pharaoh, one who “did not know Joseph”, uses this centralized power to enslave Jacob’s descendants.

The chapter ends with Jacob, near death, calling Joseph and making him swear an oath. The patriarchs are passing the covenant. Jacob will not be buried in Egypt. He will be buried in the cave of Machpelah, with Abraham and Sarah, with Isaac and Rebekah, with Leah. The covenant family does not lose its grip on the promised land even in the years of Egyptian residence. They will be sojourners, but their bones will go home.
connection: The descent into Egypt is the literal fulfillment of Genesis 15:13. God told Abram his offspring would sojourn in a foreign land for four hundred years. The journey down begins here. And God’s promise to Jacob, “I will bring you up again”, is the seed of the Exodus, the great act of redemption that will define Israel’s identity.
application: Two truths to take with you. First, when God calls you somewhere difficult, he goes with you. He told Jacob, “I myself will go down with you to Egypt.” He still goes with his people. Whatever Egypt you find yourself in, a hard season, a difficult place, an unwelcome calling, God does not stay behind. He goes. Second, your story is part of a longer story. The descent into Egypt would have looked like a tragedy to anyone watching. From God’s vantage point, it was the means by which a family became a nation. Your present descent may be the means by which God is making something larger than you can yet see.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he goes with you into every hard place.
Ask him to make you willing to leave what is familiar when he calls.
Thank him that he brings his people up again after every descent.
